stories.brief: A documentary records the development of railways in the Land of Israel, from the late nineteenth-century Jaffa–Jerusalem line through Ottoman and British rule to Israel Railways, and depicts the work of railway employees.

sources.title: People and Railways | 1978
Comrades and Enemies: The Railway Workers of Palestine
Stations in Time

storyBeats: The Jaffa–Jerusalem railway was completed in 1892, linking Jaffa’s port with Jerusalem in the Ottoman-era Land of Israel.
Jewish Jerusalem notable Yosef Navon obtained an Ottoman concession for the line in 1888 and then transferred it to a French company that raised the building funds.
The Jaffa–Jerusalem line helped move citrus for export and encouraged tourism in the years after it opened.
The Ottoman railway network also grew through lines connected to the Hejaz Railway, a major project built between 1900 and 1908 with German technical and financial support.
Under British rule, the railway system passed from Ottoman-era control into British hands; the film’s account then follows its transfer to the State of Israel.
Railway work included maintaining tracks and equipment, running stations and depots, and working in railway shops.
By 1943, more than 1,200 relatively skilled, permanent railway workers were concentrated in workshops on Haifa’s northern outskirts; many others worked around Palestine.
The workers’ jobs included driving trains, blacksmithing, and operating cranes, according to the film’s description.
The 1978 documentary presents Israel Railways as a large daily workplace, naming about 2,000 employees and describing trains carrying passengers around the country.
The documentary combines its account of the railway’s development with historical photographs from Ottoman and Mandate-era train days.

stories.brief: A 1952 Israeli newsreel follows ordinary people six months after a new economic program: a couple discusses rent, a taxi driver reports lower income, immigrants protest housing shortages, and a Tel Aviv merchant says customers are buying fewer luxuries.

sources.title: Special Report Marking Six Months of the New Economic Program
Ben Gurion Presents New Economic Policy, Investors to Benefit
Israel’s Economic Advisers, 1948–1955

storyBeats: Israel’s government announced a New Economic Policy on February 14, 1952, aiming to curb inflation and stabilize the economy.
The policy changed exchange rates for different uses, including rates connected to essential imports and foreign investment.
The policy also eased some rationing and price controls and sought to reduce demand, credit, and the government deficit.
Six months later, the newsreel marked the policy’s half-year point with newspaper headlines and short interviews with residents.
A young couple said that lower rents could make it possible for them to rent an apartment.
A taxi driver said his income had fallen as people became more careful about spending.
New immigrants at the Rehovot transition camp protested that the program had not given them homes.
An agricultural worker said he was willing to work in any kind of agricultural job that was needed.
The newsreel shows everyday activity in a grocery shop before a Tel Aviv merchant complains that customers are buying fewer luxuries, including chocolate.
At the end, the newsreel presents a child who has nothing to say about the policy.

stories.brief: A historical account describes how kibbutz communities in Israel debated private radios and teakettles in members’ rooms, once considered contrary to communal life, and how the practice changed after World War II.

sources.publisher: Zionist Organization Youth and Hechalutz Department
sources.title: Life in a Kibbutz
A History of the Kibbutz
Digging Deep Into the Collective Kitchens of Israel

storyBeats: In kibbutzim in Israel, private radios and teakettles became disputed household objects because they brought listening and tea drinking into members’ rooms.
A 1962 account says early kibbutz rooms were sparsely furnished, with a monastic simplicity.
Members were expected to meet and socialize in the shared dining room, where the community also gathered for meals.
The account describes the private kettle as more than a question of convenience: making tea in a room challenged the custom of keeping social activity in shared spaces.
A single radio in the dining room was considered enough; private radios raised similar concerns about withdrawing from communal life.
The 1962 writer says a major change in attitudes toward radios began after World War II, when kibbutz members who had served in the British Army returned.
A kibbutz federation convention allowed those veterans to use their service gratuities to furnish their rooms, including with radios and kettles.
The writer notes that some members served in the British Army for as long as six years.
A later historical account describes electric kettles arriving in family apartments and making it possible to prepare hot drinks at home, reducing the dining hall’s hold on some daily routines.
The 1962 account says that by then many kibbutzim treated radios and kettles as necessities, though limited funds meant they could not buy radios for every member.

stories.brief: A documentary records the development of railways in the Land of Israel, from the late nineteenth-century Jaffa–Jerusalem line through Ottoman and British rule to Israel Railways, and depicts the work of railway employees.

sources.title: People and Railways | 1978
Comrades and Enemies: The Railway Workers of Palestine
Stations in Time

storyBeats: The Jaffa–Jerusalem railway was completed in 1892, linking Jaffa’s port with Jerusalem in the Ottoman-era Land of Israel.
Jewish Jerusalem notable Yosef Navon obtained an Ottoman concession for the line in 1888 and then transferred it to a French company that raised the building funds.
The Jaffa–Jerusalem line helped move citrus for export and encouraged tourism in the years after it opened.
The Ottoman railway network also grew through lines connected to the Hejaz Railway, a major project built between 1900 and 1908 with German technical and financial support.
Under British rule, the railway system passed from Ottoman-era control into British hands; the film’s account then follows its transfer to the State of Israel.
Railway work included maintaining tracks and equipment, running stations and depots, and working in railway shops.
By 1943, more than 1,200 relatively skilled, permanent railway workers were concentrated in workshops on Haifa’s northern outskirts; many others worked around Palestine.
The workers’ jobs included driving trains, blacksmithing, and operating cranes, according to the film’s description.
The 1978 documentary presents Israel Railways as a large daily workplace, naming about 2,000 employees and describing trains carrying passengers around the country.
The documentary combines its account of the railway’s development with historical photographs from Ottoman and Mandate-era train days.

stories.brief: A 1952 Israeli newsreel follows ordinary people six months after a new economic program: a couple discusses rent, a taxi driver reports lower income, immigrants protest housing shortages, and a Tel Aviv merchant says customers are buying fewer luxuries.

sources.title: Special Report Marking Six Months of the New Economic Program
Ben Gurion Presents New Economic Policy, Investors to Benefit
Israel’s Economic Advisers, 1948–1955

storyBeats: Israel’s government announced a New Economic Policy on February 14, 1952, aiming to curb inflation and stabilize the economy.
The policy changed exchange rates for different uses, including rates connected to essential imports and foreign investment.
The policy also eased some rationing and price controls and sought to reduce demand, credit, and the government deficit.
Six months later, the newsreel marked the policy’s half-year point with newspaper headlines and short interviews with residents.
A young couple said that lower rents could make it possible for them to rent an apartment.
A taxi driver said his income had fallen as people became more careful about spending.
New immigrants at the Rehovot transition camp protested that the program had not given them homes.
An agricultural worker said he was willing to work in any kind of agricultural job that was needed.
The newsreel shows everyday activity in a grocery shop before a Tel Aviv merchant complains that customers are buying fewer luxuries, including chocolate.
At the end, the newsreel presents a child who has nothing to say about the policy.

stories.brief: A historical account describes how kibbutz communities in Israel debated private radios and teakettles in members’ rooms, once considered contrary to communal life, and how the practice changed after World War II.

sources.publisher: Zionist Organization Youth and Hechalutz Department
sources.title: Life in a Kibbutz
A History of the Kibbutz
Digging Deep Into the Collective Kitchens of Israel

storyBeats: In kibbutzim in Israel, private radios and teakettles became disputed household objects because they brought listening and tea drinking into members’ rooms.
A 1962 account says early kibbutz rooms were sparsely furnished, with a monastic simplicity.
Members were expected to meet and socialize in the shared dining room, where the community also gathered for meals.
The account describes the private kettle as more than a question of convenience: making tea in a room challenged the custom of keeping social activity in shared spaces.
A single radio in the dining room was considered enough; private radios raised similar concerns about withdrawing from communal life.
The 1962 writer says a major change in attitudes toward radios began after World War II, when kibbutz members who had served in the British Army returned.
A kibbutz federation convention allowed those veterans to use their service gratuities to furnish their rooms, including with radios and kettles.
The writer notes that some members served in the British Army for as long as six years.
A later historical account describes electric kettles arriving in family apartments and making it possible to prepare hot drinks at home, reducing the dining hall’s hold on some daily routines.
The 1962 account says that by then many kibbutzim treated radios and kettles as necessities, though limited funds meant they could not buy radios for every member.
